variants.title: Separate the domains
variants.context: Location and dispatch need fresh-enough data and low latency; the trip authority needs an exact transition. A nearby marker is not an available driver. A trip has one authoritative state, one version, and at most one assigned driver.
variants.prompt: Two drivers accept the same offer within milliseconds. What decides who gets the trip?
options: The versioned trip transition; the second acceptance fails the version check.
Whichever driver is closer to the pickup point when dispatch scores them.
Both drivers hold the trip until the rider picks one of them.
optionFeedback: Trip state is the authority.
Distance ranks candidates for the offer; it does not decide who owns the trip.
A trip has one driver, and leaving two holders open double-books both of them.
variants.explanation: Dispatch chooses a candidate; trip state grants ownership.

variants.title: Separate the domains
variants.context: Location and dispatch need fresh-enough data and low latency; the trip authority needs an exact transition. A nearby marker is not an available driver. A trip has one authoritative state, one version, and at most one assigned driver.
variants.prompt: The map shows a driver two blocks away. Can the rider be promised that driver?
options: Yes. The map reads the live location index, so the driver is there.
Yes, as long as the marker was refreshed within the last minute.
No. A marker can be stale, already reserved, or gone before acceptance.
optionFeedback: The index holds expiring hints; being on the map is not being available.
Age alone does not make a marker an available driver.
Markers are hints from an expiring location index.
variants.hint: What is a marker, and what is an assignment?
variants.explanation: Do not equate a nearby marker with an available driver.

variants.title: Separate the domains
variants.context: Location and dispatch need fresh-enough data and low latency; the trip authority needs an exact transition. A nearby marker is not an available driver. A trip has one authoritative state, one version, and at most one assigned driver.
variants.prompt: Why not store GPS updates and trip state in one transactional database?
options: The combined dataset would be too small to justify a second system.
A single database would serve both workloads faster than two separate systems would.
Constant location writes would contend with the records that decide assignment.
optionFeedback: Volume is not the objection; the two workloads want different guarantees.
Raw speed is not the objection; correctness for assignment is what suffers.
Location is fresh-enough data; trip state is durable business truth.
variants.hint: Which data is disposable, and which is truth?
variants.explanation: Fast spatial state proposes; the versioned trip authority decides.

variants.prompt: Each request scans an average of 40 candidate drivers at 15 requests per second. How many candidate evaluations per second?
variants.explanation: 15 × 40 = 600 candidate evaluations per second, before index-cell lookups and retries.

variants.title: Weigh the trade-off
variants.context: A larger radius improves recall but scans more candidates and can promise longer pickups; tiny cells create many index lookups; coarse cells admit false candidates. Expanding the radius cannot repair a regional supply shortage.
variants.prompt: Supply is thin, so the radius is widened. What improves and what worsens?
options: Nothing changes; the radius only affects how the map is drawn.
Recall improves; candidate scans and possible pickup distance grow.
Everything improves; more candidates also means shorter pickups.
optionFeedback: The radius sets which drivers are eligible, so it changes matches and work.
Radius trades recall for work and pickup time.
More candidates costs scan work and can hand the rider a farther driver.
variants.hint: What does a wider circle contain?
variants.explanation: A larger radius improves recall when supply is thin, but scans more candidates.

variants.title: Weigh the trade-off
variants.context: A larger radius improves recall but scans more candidates and can promise longer pickups; tiny cells create many index lookups; coarse cells admit false candidates. Expanding the radius cannot repair a regional supply shortage.
variants.prompt: Spatial cells are made extremely small. What happens?
options: Fewer false candidates, and the lookup cost stays the same.
Nothing; cell size only changes how the grid is stored.
A radius spans many cells, so index lookup overhead dominates.
optionFeedback: Precision comes at a price: the same radius now touches many more cells.
Cell size changes how many lookups a radius search performs, at both extremes.
Tiny cells create many index lookups.
variants.hint: How many cells does one radius touch now?
variants.explanation: Coarse cells admit false candidates; tiny cells multiply lookups.

variants.title: Weigh the trade-off
variants.context: A larger radius improves recall but scans more candidates and can promise longer pickups; tiny cells create many index lookups; coarse cells admit false candidates. Expanding the radius cannot repair a regional supply shortage.
variants.prompt: A region has far more requests than drivers. Will widening the radius fix wait times?
options: No. A wider radius cannot repair a regional supply shortage.
Yes. A wider radius always finds more drivers for waiting riders.
Yes, if it is combined with smaller cells for a faster search.
optionFeedback: Shortage is a supply problem, not a search problem.
Searching a wider area finds the same busy drivers; it adds no supply.
Cell size changes lookup cost, not how many drivers are on the road.
variants.explanation: Expanding the radius alone cannot repair a regional supply shortage.

variants.title: Make it idempotent
variants.context: Every retry, offer, acceptance, cancellation, and state transition is idempotent. A timeout can hide a committed assignment; query the trip by version rather than guess.
variants.prompt: A driver’s acceptance request times out. Should the app resend an acceptance blindly?
options: No. Give up on this offer and wait for dispatch to send another one.
No. Resend with the same key, since the first acceptance may have committed.
Yes. Send a fresh acceptance so the driver is not left without a trip.
optionFeedback: Giving up can abandon a trip the driver already owns, leaving the rider waiting.
Timeouts hide committed assignments.
Blind resends risk double assignment without keys.
variants.hint: What might already be true on the server?
variants.explanation: Every offer, acceptance, and cancellation is idempotent.

variants.title: Make it idempotent
variants.context: Every retry, offer, acceptance, cancellation, and state transition is idempotent. A timeout can hide a committed assignment; query the trip by version rather than guess.
variants.prompt: A cancellation event is replayed twice by the event platform. What should the consumer do?
options: Reject the trip, since a duplicate event means the state is unsafe.
Apply it once; the versioned transition makes the replay a no-op.
Run the cancellation twice so both copies of the event are honored.
optionFeedback: A replay is a transport artifact; rejecting the trip invents a new outcome.
Versioned transitions absorb replays.
The second cancellation must be a no-op, or a refund or fee is applied twice.
variants.explanation: Event consumers may be replayed; none may bypass the versioned trip transition.

variants.title: Make it idempotent

variants.prompt: Why keep history of which driver was selected and which evidence was used?
options: To explain why a transition won and to support disputes and audits.
To feed marketing dashboards about driver acceptance behavior.
It is not needed once the trip is complete and paid out.
optionFeedback: Explainability is a requirement.
Dashboards are a by-product; the requirement is explaining one assignment.
Disputes and audits arrive after the payout, and they need the evidence trail.
variants.hint: Who needs to explain an assignment later?
variants.explanation: Preserve enough history to explain which driver was selected and why a transition won.
